summary: For ages 12–13 (UK KS3, US NGSS MS-PS1-6), teach exothermic and endothermic processes operationally through the direction of temperature change: temperature up means energy transferred OUT to the surroundings (exothermic); temperature down means energy transferred IN from the surroundings (endothermic). Keep it strictly qualitative at this level — classify from measured temperature change, do not introduce enthalpy values, bond-energy sums or numerical reaction profiles. The central activity is measuring temperature before and after several reactions (and physical changes such as dissolving) and classifying each from the pupil's own data, deliberately including a surprising endothermic case so pupils don't assume all reactions release heat. An optional NGSS design extension and everyday-example matching reinforce the idea.
misconceptions: Assuming all chemical reactions give out heat, missing that some absorb it and cool the surroundings.
Reversing the terms — thinking 'exothermic' means it gets colder because energy 'exits'.
Believing 'endothermic' reactions produce cold as a substance rather than absorbing energy from the surroundings.
Confusing the reaction system with the surroundings when deciding which way energy flowed.
Thinking heating is always needed for a reaction to occur, conflating 'needs heat to start' with 'absorbs heat overall'.

activities.title: Measure, graph and classify: a temperature-change bench
steps: Choose a reaction or dissolving process (e.g. acid + alkali neutralisation, a combustion example, dissolving ammonium nitrate, or citric acid + sodium bicarbonate) and record the starting temperature. Note that dissolving is a physical change, but it still involves an energy transfer with the surroundings.

Begin the reaction or dissolving process (e.g. pour the reactants together, or stir the salt into water; a combustion example would be run as a demonstration rather than mixed in a cup) and watch the thermometer, recording temperature over time to produce a temperature–time trace.
Decide from the direction of change whether energy flowed OUT to the surroundings (temperature rose, exothermic) or IN from the surroundings (temperature fell, endothermic).
Run at least one case you expect to warm and one that unexpectedly cools (dissolving ammonium nitrate, or the sherbet reaction), and compare.
Sort each result into an 'exothermic' or 'endothermic' bin and state the rule you discovered: temperature up = energy out; temperature down = energy in.
activities.insight: Every chemical reaction — and many physical changes such as dissolving — involves an energy transfer with its surroundings, and the thermometer reading is the everyday signature of which way energy flowed. 'Mixing chemicals' can make things colder as well as hotter, because energy can be absorbed from the surroundings.

activities.title: Design a hand-warmer or cold pack to a target temperature
steps: Pick a goal: a device that gets warm (hand-warmer) or one that gets cold (instant cold pack).
Decide whether you need an exothermic or endothermic process to reach that goal, explaining the direction of energy transfer.
Assemble, test and measure the temperature your device reaches, then modify it to get closer to a target temperature.
Explain in terms of energy transfer with the surroundings why your device feels hot or cold.
activities.insight: Exothermic and endothermic processes are the basis of real devices; choosing the right direction of energy transfer lets you engineer a warming or cooling effect.

activities.title: Energy changes in changes of state, and conservation
steps: Classify melting ice and freezing water as endothermic or exothermic, justifying each by whether energy is absorbed from or released to the surroundings.
Explain how a cold pack that cools works even though 'nothing cold' was added.
State what gained the energy when the water in a cold pack cooled, using the idea that total energy is conserved.
activities.insight: Energy changes accompany physical changes (melting, freezing, dissolving) as well as dramatic reactions, and because energy is conserved, cooling means energy was transferred from the water to the dissolving/reacting system, not that 'cold' arrived.

activities.title: Sort reactions, changes and everyday devices by energy direction
steps: Sort given items — reactions, physical changes and scenarios (combustion, neutralisation, dissolving ammonium nitrate, sherbet, thermal decomposition, photosynthesis) — into exothermic and endothermic groups.
Match everyday products — hand-warmer, instant cold pack, campfire — to exothermic or endothermic, and say which way energy flows relative to you.
For a stated temperature change (e.g. 'the temperature fell'), state whether energy was absorbed or released, and predict whether a thermometer will end higher or lower.
activities.insight: The same classification rule applies across reactions, physical changes and real devices: match the direction of temperature change to the direction of energy transfer.

checkQuestion: I dissolve a spoon of ammonium nitrate in water in a cup and the cup goes noticeably COLD — this is how instant cold packs work. A student says 'something cold must be getting into the water to cool it down.' Is that what's happening — and the important part, explain in terms of energy why the cup gets cold.
checkAnswer: No cold 'gets in' — there is no such thing as cold flowing in. This is an ENDOTHERMIC change: the dissolving/reaction ABSORBS thermal energy FROM the water and surroundings, so their temperature drops. Cold is the absence of energy that has been taken away, not a substance arriving. Full marks explain the temperature fall as energy being absorbed BY the system from the surroundings.
